jordan: heads up — we've got a perf regression on the kv-prefetch path after last week's batching heuristic change. P50 latency for generationup increased ~15% on sample workload. Can someone sanity-check nsys capture flags?
jordan: trying to repro locally but nsys trace files blow up. Any tips to capture the relevant kernel timeline without 10GB files?
maya: use bracketed NVTX ranges around the exact request handling flow. That lets you use --capture-range=nvtx to only record the hot window.
maya: sample command I used: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-start=push --capture-range-end=pop -o out.nsys-rep`
sam: minor tweak: add `--sample=cpu` (or `--sample=none`) depending on whether you want sampling overhead. For tiny hot windows, sampling can drown you with noise — try without first.
zheng: if you can't instrument the code with NVTX easily, use `--capture-range=process` + `--capture-start=pid:<worker-pid>` to limit. But NVTX gives more precise brackets.
jordan: how long should the capture be? I tried 30s and the file was enormous.
maya: aim for single-request latency window + ~200ms warmup. For batching/kvcache stuff we usually do: warmup request (to fill KV cache), then bracket the actual traced request. So you might do two NVTX push/pop pairs.
sam: example pattern: `NVTX push("warmup"); do_warmup(); NVTX pop(); NVTX push("trace"); run_request(); NVTX pop();` then `nsys profile --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-start=warmup --capture-range-end=trace -o run.nsys-rep`
zheng: also use `--trace=osrt` to capture OSRT markers — kernel scheduling spikes show up there. And `--force-overwrite -o` so you don't need to babysit files.
ci-bot: Note: CI job `perf-regressions/kv-prefetch` triggered for commit 1a2b3c. Baseline artifacts available at https://ci.internal/perf/1a2b3c
jordan: after a quick run with NVTX brackets, the timeline shows lots of tiny kernel launches (~500us each) instead of fewer larger kernels. Looks like batching split logic created many small batches.
maya: yeah that pattern usually means the batching heuristic is over-eager to flush partial batches when KV handoff occurs. Two mitigations: increase max_coalesce_time, or make the handoff prefer stealing more records from next queue before spawning a kernel.
sam: for the kernel-launch overhead, try building a short capture with `--sample=none --trace=cuda` and then `nsys stats run.nsys-rep` to get kernel launch counts. If launch count >> expected, that's the sign.
zheng: another trick: use `nsys export --output=run.sqlite run.nsys-rep` then open in chrome tracing to filter by kernel duration (<1ms) to spot the scatter.
jordan: good call. Any quick filters to reduce noise in the capture?
maya: set `--trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt` but also `--cuda-memory-operations=false` if you don't care about memcopy noise. And filter by process/pid in the UI.
sam: also use `--sample-interval` / `--sample-window` if you're using sampling profiler. Longer windows reduce file size but can miss short spikes. For KV eviction investigations we prefer deterministic capture (no sampling).
zheng: when analyzing hot kernels, check grouping by name + api correlation (host call -> kernel). If you see `prefetch_kv_*` kernels frequently followed by tiny `kv_hand_off` kernels, that's the pattern.
jordan: ok will re-run bracketed capture with warmup+trace NVTXs, `--trace=cuda,nvtx,osrt`, no sampling, and `--cuda-memory-operations=false`. I'll upload the nsys-rep here.
maya: if file still big, try limiting duration by explicit NVTX delim or run single request in isolation on machine.
sam: and include `nsys status` output + `nvidia-smi` during run so we can correlate GPU load.
jordan: thanks all — uploading run.nsys-rep in ~15m. If we confirm kernel launch flood, I'll try the batching heuristic tweak and re-run. :thumbsup:
